title: EF Core, tracking & efficient queries
summary: Map objects to relational data without forgetting what the database actually does.
explanation: EF Core translates supported LINQ queries into database operations and tracks entity changes for SaveChanges. A DbContext is a short-lived unit of work and is not thread-safe. Tracking queries use an identity map; AsNoTracking avoids ordinary tracking overhead for read-only work. Migrations version the database schema.
why: An ORM reduces persistence boilerplate, but query shape, transaction boundaries, and relationship loading still determine correctness and performance.
useCase: An orders list projects a small DTO with customer name and total directly in SQL. A separate command loads a tracked order, enforces a business rule, and saves the change with a concurrency token.
whenToUse: Use tracked entities when updating a unit of work, projections or no-tracking queries for reads, and explicit transactions for operations that span multiple saves. Use raw parameterized SQL where the ORM genuinely cannot express the needed operation.
pitfalls: Sharing one context between parallel tasks.
N+1 queries from repeated or lazy relationship loading.
Applying schema migrations to production without review or deployment coordination.
bestPractices: Project early and paginate with stable ordering.
Inspect SQL and query plans for hot paths.
Use optimistic concurrency handling for conflicting edits.
simpleCode:
var customers = await database.Customers
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(customer => customer.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(customer => customer.Id)
    .Select(customer => new { customer.Id, customer.Name })
    .Take(20)
    .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
takeaways: DbContext is a unit of work, not a thread-safe global connection.
Read projections avoid unnecessary entity materialization.
An ORM does not remove the need to understand SQL.

interview.question: What is the N+1 query problem?
interview.answer: One query loads a set, then an additional query loads related data for each item. Use deliberate projections, appropriate eager loading, or batching; verify the generated SQL rather than adding Include everywhere.

interview.question: What does AsNoTracking change?
interview.answer: EF does not put ordinary query results into the context's change tracker, reducing overhead for read-only use. Updates need an explicit attach/update strategy or a separately loaded tracked entity.

quiz.question: Can two operations run concurrently on the same DbContext?
options: No, use separate contexts or serialize them
quiz.explanation: DbContext is not thread-safe. Async and no-tracking do not make concurrent use of one instance safe.

quiz.question: For a read-only API list, a good first query shape is:
options: Load all entities and filter in memory
Project needed columns and paginate in SQL
quiz.explanation: Server-side filtering and projection reduce transferred data, allocations, and unnecessary work.

title: SQL, indexes & transactions
summary: Protect invariants with database rules and make common queries cheap.
explanation: Relational tables connect through keys. Joins combine related rows. Indexes speed selected access patterns at the cost of storage and write maintenance. Transactions provide atomicity and an isolation level; the database and chosen level determine which concurrent observations are allowed. Unique constraints defend invariants even when multiple app instances race.
why: Application-only checks can race. Database constraints and transactions protect correctness, while indexes and query plans determine whether a growing application stays responsive.
useCase: A transfer debits one account and credits another atomically. A unique index rejects duplicate external payment IDs, and a composite index supports a customer's recent-order query.
whenToUse: Use transactions for changes that must succeed together. Create indexes based on real filters, joins, and sorting. Parameterize values; allowlist any dynamic identifiers that cannot be bound as parameters.
pitfalls: Adding indexes without considering write cost or leading column order.
Holding transactions open while making slow network calls.
bestPractices: Inspect execution plans with representative data.
Use unique and foreign-key constraints for data integrity.
Handle deadlocks and concurrency conflicts with bounded, appropriate retries.
takeaways: An index is a tradeoff, not free speed for every query.
Transactions and constraints protect shared data across processes.
Bind values; do not concatenate untrusted input.

interview.question: Clustered versus nonclustered index?
interview.answer: In SQL Server, a clustered index determines the table's row organization at its leaf level, while a nonclustered index is a separate structure with row locators. Details differ across database engines, so state which engine you mean.

interview.question: Why can check-then-insert still create duplicates?
interview.answer: Two transactions can both observe absence before either inserts. A unique constraint is the final arbiter; handle the conflict or use an appropriate atomic database operation.

quiz.question: What reliably prevents duplicate external payment IDs across servers?
quiz.explanation: The database can enforce uniqueness atomically for all writers, regardless of application instance.

quiz.question: What is a cost of adding an index?
quiz.explanation: Writes must maintain affected indexes, and the index consumes storage. Match indexes to important access patterns.

title: Caching & invalidation
summary: Trade freshness for speed deliberately, without mixing users or stampeding a dependency.
explanation: A cache keeps reusable results closer to callers. Cache-aside checks the cache, loads on a miss, then stores the result. IMemoryCache is process-local; a distributed cache shares entries across instances. Expiration bounds staleness but is not perfect invalidation. A cache stampede happens when many misses trigger the same expensive load.
why: Caching can reduce latency and database load, but incorrect keys or stale authorization-sensitive data can return the wrong answer quickly.
useCase: A product catalog caches public product summaries for a short interval and invalidates affected keys after edits. Tenant-specific price results include the tenant and currency in the cache key.
whenToUse: Cache expensive, frequently reused data with an acceptable staleness budget. Avoid caching user-specific data under shared keys. Use HybridCache or deliberate request coalescing when concurrent misses are a concern.
pitfalls: Treating an in-process cache as shared across servers.
Using unbounded user input as cache keys without size controls.
Caching mutable objects that callers then modify.
bestPractices: Define key scope, expiration, invalidation, and failure behavior together.
Measure hit rate and memory use.
Treat the underlying data store as the source of truth.
takeaways: Cache scope must match user, tenant, and query scope.
Freshness and invalidation are product decisions.
Coalesce expensive concurrent misses when needed.

interview.question: Memory cache versus distributed cache?
interview.answer: Memory cache is fast and local to one process, but each instance has different contents and loses them on restart. A distributed cache is shared and survives app instance replacement, but adds network and operational costs.

interview.question: What is a cache stampede?
interview.answer: Many requests miss the same key simultaneously and all load the expensive source. Request coalescing, staggered expirations, background refresh, or a library such as HybridCache can mitigate it.

quiz.question: A cache key for tenant-specific prices should include:
options: The tenant and all result-affecting dimensions
quiz.explanation: Keys must separate all inputs that can change the result, especially tenant or user scope.

quiz.question: Does IMemoryCache automatically share entries across app instances?
quiz.explanation: IMemoryCache stores entries inside one process. Cross-instance sharing needs a distributed layer.

title: Performance: measure before changing
summary: Find the bottleneck with evidence, then optimize the work that matters.
explanation: Latency measures how long one operation takes; throughput measures completed work per unit time. Percentiles reveal slow-tail behavior hidden by averages. Profilers, traces, counters, and database plans identify CPU, allocation, waiting, and query bottlenecks. A microbenchmark measures a small isolated operation, not the entire application's user experience.
why: Optimizing an insignificant loop does little when every request makes dozens of database round trips. Measurement keeps effort tied to observable improvement.
useCase: An orders endpoint has a high p95 latency. Tracing reveals N+1 queries. A projection and an appropriate index improve response time more than replacing every string concatenation.
whenToUse: Establish a representative workload and baseline before optimizing. Use BenchmarkDotNet for isolated comparisons and load tests for system behavior. Use Span<T>, pooling, or ValueTask only when measured allocation or throughput benefits justify their complexity.
pitfalls: Benchmarking Debug builds or one cold execution.
Reporting only averages and ignoring p95 or p99.
Improving throughput by allowing unbounded concurrency that overwhelms dependencies.
bestPractices: Measure before and after under comparable conditions.
Optimize algorithms, queries, and data movement before low-level tricks.
Track errors and resource usage alongside latency.
takeaways: Measure the user-visible bottleneck, not the easiest code to tweak.
Tail latency and error rates matter alongside averages.
Microbenchmarks and end-to-end load tests answer different questions.

interview.question: How would you investigate a slow API?
interview.answer: Reproduce under a representative load, examine latency percentiles and traces, identify whether time is CPU, I/O, locks, or database work, then test a focused change against the same baseline.

interview.question: When is ValueTask useful?
interview.answer: It can avoid some Task allocations in frequently synchronously completing APIs, but has more complex consumption rules and tradeoffs. Use it when measurements and the API contract justify it, not as a default replacement.

quiz.question: A low average hides occasional very slow requests. Inspect:
quiz.explanation: High percentiles and traces expose slow-tail behavior and help locate the responsible work.

quiz.question: Before introducing object pooling, you should:
options: Measure allocation pressure and ownership risks
quiz.explanation: Pooling adds lifetime and correctness complexity. It is useful only when the measured benefit justifies those costs.
